Workshop 1 · Sessions 1–2 · Thursday 1 October 2026

Text is data: regex for information extraction

We start with the oldest tool in NLP and still one of the most used: regular expressions. By the end of the day you will have pulled failure times, prices and complaints out of 30,000 reviews, and built a redactor that strips personal data from a support inbox.

Open slides Notebooks and data Practice problems

By the end of this workshop you can

  • write regular expressions using character classes, quantifiers, anchors, alternation and groups
  • apply them at scale with Python's re module and pandas .str methods
  • measure a pattern's precision and recall, and choose which one matters for a business use
  • explain what regex cannot do, and why that motivates the rest of the course

Course outcome CO1 · Reading: [SLP] Chapter 2

2. Why text, why managers?

Most of the data a company creates is unstructured: product reviews, support tickets, call transcripts, emails, contracts, social posts. None of it fits into a spreadsheet as it stands, and so most of it goes unread. Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the set of methods that turn this text into something you can count, compare, search and predict.

You won't be writing production NLP systems in your job. You will be commissioning, buying and judging them. To do that well you need to know what each technique does, what it gets wrong, and how to tell whether it is working. That is why every method in this course is worked by hand before we code it.

3. Regular expressions in five minutes

A regular expression ("regex") is a pattern that describes a set of strings. For example, \d{6} means "six digits in a row", which describes every Indian PIN code (and plenty of other numbers). Regexes are used everywhere from web forms to log files to data-privacy tools, and they are usually the first step in any NLP pipeline.

The key idea for this workshop is that a pattern can be right in two ways and wrong in two ways. Say you want every review that complains about noise, and you search for loud. Each review then lands in one of four boxes:

Review is about noise Review is not about noise
Pattern matches True positive (TP): "a very loud hum" False positive (FP): "cloudy water"
Pattern doesn't match False negative (FN): "it's so noisy" True negative (TN): "fits perfectly"

Positive or negative is what the pattern said (match or no match). True or false is whether it was right. So a false positive is a wrong match, and a false negative is a miss.

Two numbers summarise the boxes:

  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Of the reviews you matched, what share really are about noise?
  • Recall = TP / (TP + FN). Of the reviews that really are about noise, what share did you find?

For example, out of 1,000 reviews, 50 are about noise. Your pattern matches 40, and 30 of those are right. That gives TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 20 and TN = 940, so precision is 30/40 = 75% and recall is 30/50 = 60%. Notice that TN appears in neither formula. Almost every review is a true negative, so counting them would make any pattern look good: this one is "97% accurate" while missing 40% of the complaints.

Making a pattern stricter reduces false positives, which raises precision. Making it looser reduces false negatives, which raises recall. Most of regex work, and much of NLP evaluation, comes down to managing this trade-off.

4. Read

  • [SLP] Jurafsky & Martin, Chapter 2: the sections on regular expressions (basic patterns, disjunction, grouping, precedence, the worked example, substitution and capture groups). Skim the rest; tokenisation is Workshop 2.

5. Look at the data in Excel (about 10 min)

Before writing any code, look at the raw data the way a manager would. Follow Looking at the data in Excel to open copies of reviews.csv.gz and support_inbox.csv, then:

  • Reviews: filter rating to 1 and read ten or so text cells. Note what you would want as spreadsheet columns, such as prices, model numbers, "stopped working after 3 months" or noise complaints. In class you will pull these out with regex. Also look for leftovers such as <br />.
  • Support inbox: compare a few text cells with the gold_… columns next to them. These columns are the answer key you will score your patterns against in W01-B.

6. Practise: regex basics (about 25 min)

Open ADS6703/w01/W01-0-regex-basics.ipynb and work through it. It covers the regex syntax the in-class notebooks assume, one idea at a time, each with a short self-checking exercise: character classes, quantifiers, anchors and word boundaries, groups, substitution and lookarounds.

7. Practise: pandas basics (about 25 min)

Open ADS6703/w01/W01-0b-pandas-basics.ipynb. It covers the pandas the in-class notebooks use, on a table of eight reviews: selecting columns, filtering rows with True/False masks, .loc, counting, the .str methods that run a regex over a whole column, .apply, groupby, and loading the real data. If you already use pandas, skim the cheat sheet at the end and do the five exercises.

8. Try (optional, 10 min)

Open regex101.com, set the flavour to Python, and paste in this text:

Fits my Whirlpool WDT970SAHZ0. Paid $24.99, Sears wanted $80!
Stopped working after 3 months. Call 98229 67803 or mail a.rao@gmail.com.

Try to write patterns that match (1) the prices, (2) the model number, and (3) "3 months". The panel on the right explains each part of your pattern as you type.

Handout: regex cheat sheet

Print this page, or keep it open during the labs.

What to match

abc literal text
[abc] one of a, b, c
[a-z0-9] a range
[^0-9] anything except a digit
. any character (except newline)
\d \D digit / not a digit
\w \W word character [A-Za-z0-9_] / not
\s \S whitespace / not
\$ \. \( \+ escape special characters

How many

? 0 or 1
* 0 or more
+ 1 or more
{n} exactly n
{n,m} n to m
*? +? lazy: as few as possible

Where

^ $ start / end of string
\b word boundary

Choices and groups

a|b a or b
(…) capturing group
(?:…) non-capturing group
(?i) ignore case
(?<!x) not preceded by x
(?!x) not followed by x

Python and pandas

Python re pandas (whole column) Returns
re.search(p, s) s.str.contains(p) first match / True–False per row
re.findall(p, s) s.str.findall(p) list of all matches (only the groups, if the pattern has any)
m.group(1) s.str.extract(p) capturing groups → columns
re.sub(p, r, s) s.str.replace(p, r, regex=True) text with replacements

Always write patterns as raw strings, r"\d+". Add case=False in pandas, or flags=re.I in re, to ignore case.

Scoring a pattern

TP (true positive) = a correct match · FP (false positive) = a wrong match · FN (false negative) = a miss. See the four boxes in the pre-read.

Precision = TP / (TP + FP) Of what I matched, how much was right? Raise it by making the pattern stricter.
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) Of what I should have matched, how much did I find? Raise it by making the pattern looser.
F1 = 2PR / (P + R) A single score that balances the two.
